div.p: Multiprocessor systems are increasingly being used in real-time computing, and much research has been done on schedulability analysis of these systems. However, current schedulability analyses have only limited support for joblevel parallelism (JLP): jobs are typically restricted to a simple parallel structure, and malleable jobs, where the number of processors assigned to a job is dynamic, is not widely supported. This paper presents a framework for analyzing systems with malleable jobs of an arbitrary parallel structure. A fair intra-job scheduler is assumed, allowing the state of a job to be represented by a scalar and its parallel structure to be modeled as a function. It is demonstrated that jobs executing their worst-case computations do not necessarily constitute a worst-case scenario with respect to schedulability. This implies that exact schedulability analysis will not be sustainable. Upper bounds on interference and demand are developed. This framework is then used to construct a pessimistic, but sustainable schedulability test for systems scheduled with EDF. The EDF test has poor worst-case performance, but does allow schedulability analysis for a class of systems for which no other analysis currently exists. We believe the framework itself could also be used to construct analyses with better performance.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Multiprocessor systems have become widespread in realtime applications, and much research has been done in the recent years on schedulability analysis of these systems. So far, however, most analyses of multiprocessor systems do not allow job-level parallelism, where multiple processors may be used to simultaneously execute a single job. The analyses that do support JLP have strict limitations to their applicability, such as not supporting malleable jobs, or limiting the parallel structure allowed by each job.

In a previous paper [10] we discussed fundamental prop-erties of scheduling malleable jobs with an arbitrary parallel structure. The intra-job scheduler was assumed to be workconserving, but otherwise undefined. Several observations of anomalous temporal behavior were made, including the following:

1. Assuming worst-case execution for each parallel branch of a job does not represent a worst-case scenario for the job as a whole: There exist situations where a job is guaranteed to complete if executing its full worst-case computation, but is no longer guaranteed to complete if executing less.
2. The intra-job scheduling decision that leads to the earliest completion of a job may depend on the number of processors assigned to the job in the future.

These observations make schedulability analysis difficult without somehow restricting either the intra-job scheduler, or the parallel structure allowed by each job. This research is motivated by the development of an experimental programming language called "Toc" [12], which has structured specification of timing requirements and parallelism as a core feature. Toc is based on occam/CSP, and the process-oriented programming paradigm [e.g. 13], where dividing a program into multiple parallel processes is a way of organizing and structuring the program, not only a means of achieving parallelism. Restricting the parallel structure of process-oriented programs is therefore undesirable. Process-oriented programs are not widely used in real-time applications, in part because analyses do not support these parallel structures.

Toc, occam, and other languages such as Google Go, use lightweight processes that are not mapped directly onto operating system threads. Switching between these processes is fast [15], and the number of such processes can be several magnitudes higher than the number of tasks in traditional real-time systems. In this paper, these properties are exploited by assuming a fair intra-job scheduler, which means that the parallel branches of a job will be assumed to always progress at the same speed. If there are sufficient processors assigned to the job to execute all branches, then all branches will progress at full speed; if there are fewer processors, say m processors and n parallel branches, then all branches will progress at m/n of their full speed. This is an idealization that can only be realized by switching infinitely fast between branches. However, the errors introduced by this assumption will be limited by taking a into account a certain amount of skew.

The fair intra-job scheduler assumption allows the state, i.e. how far the job has come in its execution, to be represented by a scalar, and the parallel structure of a job to be modeled as a function. The intra-job scheduler is also simple to express mathematically, and allows analyses that circumvent the timing anomalies described above.

div.head: Contributions
div.p: This paper introduces a framework for schedulability analysis of malleable jobs with an arbitrary parallel structure by assuming a fair intra-job scheduler. An upper bound on tolerable interference is presented, together with an upper bound on the demand of a job during windows of time that ends with a deadline for the job. This framework is then used to develop a rudimentary schedulability analysis for systems scheduled with EDF.

div.head: Organization
div.p: Section 2 specifies the basic notation used in the paper, briefly summarizes multiprocessor schedulability analysis, and then provides examples of temporal anomalies that may occur when jobs are allowed an arbitrary parallel structure. Section 3 describes the job model and the intra-job scheduling model. Section 4 discusses schedulability, worst-case execution times and sustainability of schedulability analysis for the tasking model of this paper. Section 5 derives a sufficient condition for when a job meets its deadline, based on the interference from other jobs and the maximum skew of the intra-job scheduler. Also derived is an upper bound on the interference to a job as a function of the demand of higher priority jobs, and an upper bound on the demand of a job for a given window in time. In section 6 these bounds are used to construct a schedulability analysis for systems scheduled with EDF.

div.head: Notation and Terminology
div.p: The term job will be used for any computation with a release time and a deadline. Jobs will be denoted with lowercase letters. The absolute release time and deadline of a job a is denoted r a and d a , respectively. A task is a repeating job. Tasks are denoted with upper-case letters; the minimum inter-release time of jobs from a task A is denoted T A , and the relative deadline of A with respect to its release is denoted D A . The set of tasks is denoted T.
Throughout the paper, the number of processors in the system will be denoted m. Homogeneous systems are assumed, meaning that all processors are considered identical.

The parallel structure of a job will be described with a syntax similar to that of the programming language occam [14]. In occam and its derivatives, multiple statements are explicitly specified whether to execute in sequence using the sequence operator (SEQ), or in parallel using the parallel operator (PAR). The structure built up by the nested use of SEQ and PAR serves both as a programming language mechanism, and as an execution model.
A parallel construct does not terminate before all branches terminate. For example, if a job has the following structure:
div.formula: SEQ PAR A B C
div.p: then the computation in A and B may execute in parallel, while the computation in C may begin execution once both A and B are completed. In this paper, the pseudo-code process Exec(t) will denote a job component that requires t time units of serial execution. We will say that two jobs have the same structure, if they can be written so that they only differ by the values of t in the Exec(t) statements.

The scheduler that distributes the processors of the system to its jobs is called the job scheduler. In this paper, the job scheduler is considered to output a schedule for each job, which is denoted e(t), and is the number of processors assigned to the job as a function of time relative to the release of the job. This schedule is in general not predictable, e.g. because it depends on the arrival of jobs from sporadic tasks. The scheduling decision made by the job scheduler must take the differing real-time requirements of the jobs into account when determining the schedule.

The intra-job scheduler is the scheduler that distributes the processors assigned to each job to the parallel branches of that job. The intra-job scheduler is not a real-time scheduler, as there is no difference in real-time requirements between the branches of a single job. The separation between the job scheduler and the intra-job scheduler is a logical abstraction; it may well be the same scheduler.

A scheduler is classified as work-conserving, if it does not leave processors idle if there exists ready work to be done. A job scheduler is priority driven if jobs have a fixed relative priority; this includes EDF where jobs, but not tasks, have a fixed relative priority. A coscheduler is a job scheduler for systems with JLP, which allocates as many processors as possible to the highest priority job; then allocates any remaining processors to the second highest priority job, and so on. It is usually not possible to determine the actual computation time of a job in advance. Therefore, a safe upper bound on the worst-case execution time (WCET) of a job is used instead. Because WCETs are always upper bounds, an analysis should be able to handle jobs that use less time than expected, without making the system unschedulable. An analysis is sustainable [2] if a system determined to be schedulable remains schedulable when decreasing its required work or relaxing its timing requirements. A schedulability analysis is called exact if it provides sufficient and necessary conditions for schedulability; or pessimistic if it only provides sufficient conditions.

div.head: Multiprocessor Schedulability Analysis
div.p: Schedulability analysis of most uniprocessor fixed priority systems may take advantage of a property known as the critical instant, which states that if a job from a task meets its deadline when released simultaneously with all other tasks, then it will always meet its deadline. A slightly weaker property applies to EDF, which states that if the synchronous release of all tasks does not eventually lead to a deadline miss, then no other release patterns will lead to a deadline miss.

For multiprocessors there is no general way of identify-ing a critical instant. Instead, the general approach is to find an upper bound on the amount of work required by a job during all possible windows of a given length; and comparing this to a lower bound on the amount of work that must interfere with a job to make it unschedulable. Two well-known schedulability analyses for multiprocessor EDF are the BAK-test [1] and the BCL-test [5]. Based on the system to be analyzed one test may perform better than the other. An iterative approach for EDF using response time analysis is found in [4]. None of these analyses support job-level parallelism. This paper will use the classification of systems with JLP that is given in [7]. Here, a parallel job is defined to be rigid, if the number of processors required by the job is determined a-priori, moldable if it is determined by the scheduler, but does not change during the execution of the job, or malleable if the number of processors assigned to the job may change during the execution of the job. A task is defined to be rigid if all its jobs are rigid, and so on. Schedulability analyses of rigid tasks can be found in e.g. [7] and [9].

Analyses of JLP systems typically restrict the parallel structure allowed by a task. The analysis given in [8] assumes that all jobs are fully parallelizable. The analysis in [11] assumes that jobs have a basic fork-join structure, where the main thread of a job may fork into multiple branches, but where the branches themselves are not allowed to fork. A similar constraint is used in [3], where jobs with this structure are called multi-phase jobs. The analysis in [6] allows costs to be added to the parallelization of a job, but does not consider the parallel structure of the program the job implements.

div.head: Jobs with Arbitrary Parallel Structure
div.p: In [10] we discuss fundamental properties of the schedulability of jobs with an arbitrary parallel structure. Examples of timing anomalies were observed. Two of these observations will be repeated in this section, and examples will be given.
Observation 1. There exist situations where a job is guaranteed to complete on a schedule if executing its full worstcase computation, but may no longer be guaranteed to complete if executing less.

This observation is the result of using a work-conserving but otherwise undefined intra-job scheduler. A precise description is this: Let a be a parallel job and s a schedule, so that a will complete on s for any work-conserving intra-job scheduler. For certain choices of a and s, however, a will no longer complete on s for all schedulers if computation is removed from a.

div.head: Example 1
div.p: Let a be a job with the computation shown in Fig. 1a and s be the schedule in Fig. 1e. In the interval 0 ≤ t < 1, a has two parallel branches and is given two processors. A workconserving scheduler will execute both branches, leading to the computation depicted in Fig. 1c. In the interval 1 ≤ t < 2, a has four parallel branches and is given four processors. Therefore, a is guaranteed to complete by t = 2.

Say the computation of a was overestimated, and a in reality has the structure shown in Fig. 1b; this happens if the fourth Exec(1) turns out to be Exec(0). For 0 ≤ t < 1 there are now two processors and three parallel branches. An undefined, but work-conserving scheduler now has a choice. One of these choices results in the remaining computation at t = 1 shown in Fig 1d. This computation has a sequential restriction, and will not complete by t = 2.

Observation 1 implies that, even if the schedule is known, schedulability analysis will not be sustainable unless the scheduler is better defined. However, the next observation illustrates the difficulty of defining a better scheduler.

Observation 2. The intra-job scheduling decision that leads to the earliest completion of a job may depend on the number of processors assigned to it in the future. This observation is based on the following fact: A job a that has many parallel threads requiring little computation is incomparable with respect to schedulability to a job b with few parallel threads requiring much computation, even if C a > C b . If the job is given many processors for a short time, then a may complete while b may not; if the job is given few processors for a long time, then b may complete while a may not. As there exists jobs that end up as type-a or type-b depending on choices made by the intra-job scheduler, and as the intra-job scheduler cannot in general predict the number of processors available in the future, there exist decisions that are neither correct nor wrong at the time they are made.

div.head: Example 2
div.p: Consider the job given in Fig. 2a and the schedules given in Fig. 2f. The schedules are identical up to t = 2. In the interval 0 ≤ t < 1, the job contains two parallel branches, but is given only one processor, so the scheduler must make a decision as to when each of the two branches gets to execute. Fig. 2b and Fig. 2c depict the remaining computation at time t = 1 if only executing the first, or if only executing the second branch, respectively.

For the interval 1 ≤ t < 2 the job is given three processors. The remaining computation at t = 2 will be that depicted in Fig. 2d or 2e if the first choice was that of Fig. 2b or 2c, respectively. It can be seen that the computation depicted in Fig. 2d is schedulable with s 1 but not s 2 , while the computation depicted in Fig. 2e is schedulable with s 2 but not s 1 .

div.head: Tasking Model
div.p: To allow analysis, the intra-job scheduler must be better defined. For this paper, we will assume a fair intra-job scheduler. Then, all branches of a job will progress at the same speed, so the state of a job can be represented by a scalar v, which will be called the virtual time. The parallel structure of a job can then be represented by a function c(v), which will be called the computation function of the job.

div.head: Basic Assumptions
div.p: Jobs will be assumed to have a SEQ/PAR-structure. We will assume that the only synchronization between branches within a job is due to sequential no other synchronization within a job, apart from the implicit synchronization imposed by the sequence operator.

Time will be modeled as a real number, i.e. t ∈ R. Timing in computer systems is more accurately modeled as discrete, as argued in e.g. [4], but assuming continuous time allows a wider range of mathematical analysis to be used.

For the EDF analysis we will require constrained deadlines, i.e. D A ≤ T A for all tasks A ∈ T. Furthermore, an ideal system model will be assumed, with no jitter and no cost of preemptions. It will also be assumed that jobs are independent. Although the latter is an unrealistic assumption, results from the independent case should be a useful starting point for analyzing systems with interacting jobs.

div.head: Computation Functions and Virtual Time
div.p: Definition 1 (Computation Function). The computation function c(v) of a job denotes the maximum number of processors that the job can utilize at virtual time v for that job.
The computation function of a job is equivalent to the number of processors used by a job as a function of time, given that the job is always given as many processors as it can utilize.
For c(v) to be a valid computation function there must exist a P so that
div.formula: c(v) > 0 when 0 ≤ v ≤ P c(v) = 0 otherwise (1)
div.p: The parameter P is the minimum completion time of the job, and is the required time for a job to complete if it is always given as many processors as it can utilize. The total computational requirement of a job, C, can then be defined as a function of c(v): Definition 2 (Virtual Time). The virtual time of a job is denoted v(t) and is the amount of time required to reach the current point of execution if the job is always given as many processors as it can utilize. v(t) is described by the following equations:
div.formula: C = ∞ 0 c(v) dv = P 0 c(v) dv(2)
v(r) = 0 d dt v(t) = min s(t) c(v(t)) , 1(3)
div.p: where r is the release time of the job, and s(t) is the number of processors available for the job at time t. If c(v) = 0 then d dt v(t) is defined to be 0. The execution of a job is complete when v(t) = P , since there is no more remaining computation. Virtual time follows real-time whenever a task is allowed as many processors as it can utilize, and slows down when fewer processors are available.
For all t, v(t) is continuous and monotonously increasing.

div.head: Skew
div.p: The fair intra-job scheduler is an idealization that is not perfectly realizable in a real system. If an intra-job scheduler allows some branches to advance more than others then this is called skew.

When the scheduler is perfectly fair, a job that gets to execute will show some progress; when the scheduler is skewed this is no longer the case. For example if the scheduler does not execute the branch with the longest serial part, then even though the job executes it may not decrease the minimum completion time of the remaining computation.

The skew is assumed to be bounded by a number σ, such that for any window of length L, a branch is allowed to execute at most L • σ more than another branch. This means that for a job a that meets its deadline, skew in the intrajob scheduler will contribute at most σ • (d a -r a ) to the completion time of a.

div.head: Reducing Computation Functions
div.p: The computation function of a job is independent of the number of processors in the system, only on the structure and execution times of the parallel branches of the job. However, no job will ever be given more than m processors simultaneously, and to simplify the later analysis of this paper it is convenient that c(v) ≤ m for all v. A reduced computation function is a function where c(v) ≤ m for all v, and which behaves equivalently with the original function in systems of m processors.

A reduced computation function can be interpreted as the number of processors used by the job as a function of time since the release of the job, given that there are no other jobs in the system. As long as computation functions are reduced, virtual time will follow real time when there is no interference from other jobs. Without reduced computation functions, virtual time may slow down due to limitations of the system itself.
A computation function c(v) can be reduced to m processors by computing
div.formula: c m (t) = min{c(v(t)), m}(4)
div.p: using Eq. 3 with s(t) = m. Informally, a reduced computation function is found by limiting all sections of the function where c(t) > m to m, and extending them by a factor of c(t)/m, conserving the total amount of computation in the section. For the rest of this paper it will be assumed that all computation functions are reduced.

div.head: Sustainability
div.p: When going from scalar computation times to computation functions, certain scheduling analysis concepts must be redefined in order to discuss sustainability. First, consider the following questions: If one compares two alternative jobs a and b, with identical releases and deadlines, what does it mean that 1. the computation required by b is an upper bound to the computation required by a, 2. a is easier to schedule than b,
3. b has a higher demand than a, and thus may cause more interference to lower priority jobs.
For systems without JLP, these statements are all equivalent to C a ≤ C b .
For the model in this paper, however, these questions are independent. The next section will provide the necessary definitions:

div.head: Definitions
div.p: First, consider the concept of upper bounds on computation.

Definition 3 (Upper Bound on Computation). For a job b, if there exists a job a that has the same structure as b, but with a less or equal amount of computation, then c b (v) is said to be an upper bound of c a (v).
div.formula: If c b (v) is an upper bound of c a (a), then c a (v) is called a reduction of c b (v).
div.p: All computation times derived from actual programs are worst-case estimates. Therefore, in an actual execution of a job, any or all of the branches in the job may require less than their expected computation. A consequence is that even if execution time analysis of a job b leads to a computation function of c b (v), the only thing known about an actual execution of b is that it will behave as if having some computation function for which c b (v) is an upper bound.
Second, consider what it means for a job to be easier to schedule than another.

Definition 4 (Easier to schedule). For two jobs a and b, with identical release and deadline, a is easier to schedule than b, iff for all schedules In other words, a is easier to schedule than b, if b meeting its deadline in some schedule implies that a will also meet its deadline if given the same schedule.

div.p: Third, consider the demand of a job.
Definition 5 (Demand). The demand of a job a in a window [t 0 , t 1 ] is denoted D a (t 0 , t 1 ) and is given by

div.p: The demand of a job is the total amount of execution performed by the job in the given window, and is dependent on the schedule.

div.head: Non-Sustainability of Exact Analysis
div.p: The fair intra-job scheduler does not eliminate the temporal anomaly described in Observation 1, where a job would complete on a given schedule if executing its full worst-case computation, but may no longer complete if executing less:

div.head: Example 4
div.p: Let a and b be the jobs in in Fig. 1a and1b, respectively. Because b has the same structure as a, but with less computation, c b (v) is a reduction of c a (v).

Let the jobs both be given the schedule depicted in Fig. 1e. Virtual time when executing the two jobs is shown in Fig. 4. Job a completes at t = 2. Job b executes a reduction of c a (v), but does not complete until t ≈ 2.33.
If c a (v) was a WCET estimate of c b (v), and the deadline was 2, then the job would meet its deadline if executing its full worst-case computation, but may miss its deadline if executing less.

A similar anomaly may occur due to interference to a low priority job from a high priority job. This is illustrated in the following observation: Observation 3. Lower priority jobs may miss their deadlines when the computation of a higher priority job is reduced. Job b is given a higher priority than job a; this is necessary for b to meet its deadline given its worst-case computation. For b there are no higher priority jobs, and b always completes at or before its deadline of t = 4.
Job a suffers interference from b. If b executes its upper bound, then the virtual time of a progresses as shown in Fig. 6a, and a completes at t = 2.5, meeting its deadline.

If b executes c red (t) instead, which is a reduction of its upper bound, then the virtual time of a progresses as shown in Fig. 6b. Job a suffers a more interference, and does not complete until t = 3, missing its deadline. Observation 3 implies that exact schedulability analysis cannot be sustainable for the tasking model in this paper: The system in Example 5 is in fact schedulable when jobs execute their WCET, so an exact schedulability analysis must deem the system schedulable. On the other hand, the system is in fact not schedulable in some cases where jobs execute less, so a sustainable analysis cannot deem the system schedulable.
Observation 3 pertains to a wide range of job schedulers; nothing is assumed except for the existence of two jobs with a fixed relative priority.

div.head: Upper Bounds on Interference and Demand
div.p: A low priority job may suffer interference from higher priority jobs. In this section we will derive an upper bound on this interference as a function of the total demand of higher priority jobs. Then, an upper bound on the demand of a job will be given for windows that end with the deadline of the job. It will be shown that these upper bounds are also valid if computations are reduced.

div.head: Upper Bound on Demand
div.p: The bound in Theorem 1 is useful for schedulability analysis, because it is independent of the structures of both the delayed and the interfering jobs, and only depends on the total amount of demand from the higher priority jobs. It is also sustainable with respect to decrease in computation, in the sense that if a maximum interference is found using Theorem 1, then this bound also holds if computation is removed from the low priority job.
However, in order to obtain a sustainable analysis for the whole system, a sustainable demand bound of higher priority jobs must also be found.

div.p: When computation is removed from a parallel structure, this may have one of two effects on the computation function for a given v: That it is reduced, or that it is increased because part of the computation is shifted leftwards from higher values of v. Because the upper limit for the integral is P a , there is no remaining computation that can shift into the integral, but computation may shift out of it. Therefore, the value of the integral cannot decrease when computation is reduced.

Theorem 2. Let a be a job with deadline at d a . Let D ub (t 0 , d a ) be an upper bound on the demand in the window [t 0 , d a ] for job a if executing its worst-case computation or a reduction of this. Then, for all schedules where a meets its deadline, and all t 0 ≤ d a ,
div.formula: D ub (t 0 , d a ) ≤ P a P a -(d a -t 0 ) c a (v ) dv(25)
div.p: Proof. The demand from a in a fixed window ending with a deadline of a obtains its maximum when a begins as late as possible. If a meets its deadline, a may begin executing no later than t = d a -p a , in which case it must execute with
From the definition of demand (Eq. 6), we get

div.p: For negative values of v, c a (v) = 0 by definition, so the max function can be removed:
div.formula: D ub (t 0 , d a ) ≤ P a P a -(d a -t 0 ) c a (v ) dv(28)
div.p: Finally, using Lemma 3 it can be seen that this bound also holds for reductions of c a (v).

div.head: Schedulability Analysis for EDF
div.p: In this section, the framework from the previous sections will be used to demonstrate a sustainable schedulability analysis for systems using an EDF. We will assume that the job-level scheduler is an EDF coscheduler.

The strategy is as follows: For each task we find an upper bound on demand during any window ending with a deadline for the task, using Theorem 2. This bound also holds when replacing the task computations with reductions.

With EDF, for a job a, only jobs with deadlines earlier than d a may interfere with a. Using this, we then find an upper bound on the total demand from other tasks that may interfere with a. Finally, Theorem 1 is used to limit the interference caused by this demand. If the interference is sufficiently small then a will meet its deadline.

When analyzing tasks instead of jobs, it helps to extend computation functions so that they become periodic: Definition 7. The T -period extension of a computation function c(v) is denoted c (v, T ) and is given by
div.formula: c (v, T ) = c (v -v/T T ) (29)
div.p: Lemma 4. The demand W from a task X in a window of length L from jobs with deadlines within the window, satisfies
div.formula: W ≤ P X P X -L c X (v, T X ) dv (30)
div.p: where c X (v) is an upper bound to the computation functions of all jobs of X. Proof. Using a strategy from [4], the jobs from task X that may execute within a window is divided into three categories: 1. jobs with release and deadline within the window, which contributes at most a full C X of demand, 2. a maximum of one job with deadline outside the window, which by definition of W does not contribute to demand, and 3. a maximum of one job with release outside the window, which contributes up to C X of demand, depending on the window alignment. An illustration is given in Fig. 8, with one job from each category. A job with deadline outside of the window does not contribute to the demand, so the demand can never decrease by shifting the alignment of the task forward until a job deadline coincides with the end of the window. The demand from a job released outside the window is maximized by assuming that it executes as late as possible, completing execution at its deadline. Note that this assumption has no effect on the demand from jobs completely within the window. An upper bound on demand can therefore be found when the deadline of a job aligns with the end of the interval, with all earlier jobs released as late as possible. An illustration of the worst-case is given in Fig. 9.
A demand bound is then found by taking the sum of the contributions. Say the window is (t 0 , t 1 ). Let the first job be denoted x, and the first job deadline d. The worst-case demand then satisfies
div.formula: W ≤ D x (t 0 , d) + L T X C X (31)

div.head: Discussion
div.p: As shown, the EDF schedulability test of Theorem 3 has a worst-case utilization arbitrarily close to 0. This bound is derived from one particular task set, and requires an infinitely long task period. It should be noted that this limit is caused by pessimism in the test; the task set used in the example is actually schedulable. The task model in this paper is a superset of traditional multiprocessor EDF, which has an actual worst-case utilization arbitrarily close to 1.

The pessimism of the EDF test has several causes. Theorem 1 is pessimistic in that it assumes that demand from higher priority jobs align in the worst possible way. For example, if there is one low and one high priority job each requiring one processor, and m ≥ 2, then demand from the high priority job will not cause interference. However, Theorem 1 yields an interference bound of W/m. Theorem 2 is not pessimistic in itself, as it is possible for a job to yield the demand given in the theorem. The main source of pessimism is the EDF test itself, which assumes that all higher priority jobs start as late as possible and finish at the same deadline. It should be possible to use Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 to to construct less pessimistic tests, perhaps by using iterated response-time analysis, as done in [4].

Another point to consider is whether or not to allow joblevel parallelism at all. It is always possible to suppress JLP by serializing all jobs. If the resulting increase in response times is acceptable and does not cause deadlines to be missed, then this serialization can make task sets schedulable that are not schedulable when JLP is enabled. This is also discussed in [11], where job-level parallelism is suppressed for all jobs where it is not required for the job to meet its deadline.

However, when job-level parallelism is indeed required, and the jobs to be analyzed has a complex parallel structure, then the schedulability test in this paper can be used. To our knowledge, no other existing analysis methods support malleable jobs with a complex parallel structure.

The schedulability test is based on several assumptions, which to various degrees are sources of error: 1. Tasks are independent, 2. no cost of preemptions, 3. fair scheduler, with error bounded by skew variable, and 4. the system uses continuous time.
The first assumption severely limits the usefulness of the analysis for practical systems, but does not affect the validity of the analysis for systems where tasks actually are independent.

The second assumption is a source of error. Preemption causes jitter, and causes jobs to slow down because of cache misses etc. This should be taken into account. If an upper bound on the number of preemptions can be determined in advance, and an upper bound on the cost of each preemption can also be found, then the analysis can be modified to accommodate this cost.

The third assumption requires that a maximum value of skew can be found for the intra-job scheduler, so that the total skew is linear with time. This is an assumption that is not likely to hold for short windows of time, because it again would require an infinitely fast scheduler. There probably exists better models for skew. However, for this paper, total skew is only computed for windows from the release to the deadline for a job, which should of sufficient length to minimize the errors of the model itself.

The continuous time assumption is primarily required to prove the interference bound in Theorem 1. We believe it should be possible to incorporate the errors of this assumption as part of the errors caused by skew.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: This paper has introduced a framework for analyzing malleable jobs with an arbitrary parallel structure, by using a fair intra-job scheduler. The notion of upper bounds on computation is discussed for these systems, and it is demonstrated that jobs executing the upper bound of computation does not necessarily represent a worst-case scenario.

An upper bound of interference as a function of demand from higher priority jobs was derived, as well as an upper bound on demand from a job for windows that end with a deadline for the job. These bounds were used to construct an EDF schedulability test. This test is fairly simple, and has poor worst-case performance. However, it does allow analysis for a class of systems for which no existing analysis methods currently apply. We also believe the framework could be used as a starting point for more advanced analysis.
